extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in media policy, journalists, researchers, and media activists
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and documenting the concentration of ownership, revenue, and influence across U.S. media sectors (movies, TV, radio, newspapers, magazines, books, cable, internet) using Bagdikian's 50% rule and related indicators. The page presents metrics, sector-specific examples, regulatory drivers, and democratic implications of consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50% threshold for dominance (Bagdikian method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The biggest companies whose combined market share exceeded 50 percent of their sector were counted as the dominant media corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by Bagdikian in 1983 and subsequent updates; applied across sectors to produce a single 'number of corporations' dominating information and ideas. Example: counting how many firms together control half the revenue or circulation in a sector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure dominance by revenue (or circulation for newspapers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use revenue figures to determine which companies dominate a media sector. For newspapers, Bagdikian originally used circulation where revenue data were unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer revenue when available (Advertising Age data used for 2009). Note the methodological caveat that using circulation vs revenue can change the assessed dominance; the author argues revenue typically reveals even fewer dominant owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising revenue concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration of advertising spending is a key indicator of commercial influence across media; high aggregate ad spending and its concentration signal commercial model dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $309 billion spent on ads in 2009; two companies (Google and Yahoo) received over half of online advertising revenue in 2009. Use ad-revenue shares to assess which firms command the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: motion pictures (box office share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the share of box office receipts captured by major studios to assess film-industry concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 Warner Brothers, Paramount, Sony/Columbia and 20th Century Fox accounted for more than 60% of the $10.6 billion box office; six studios together took 80% in 2009. Use box-office revenue shares to identify dominant studios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: newspapers (circulation/revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify chains that together account for over half of newspaper circulation or revenue to assess newspaper ownership concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 five corporations received over half the newspaper industry's $19.7 billion revenues (Gannett, Tribune, New York Times Co., Advance Publications, MediaNews Group). Note earlier practice used circulation when revenue was unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: magazines (ad revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the number of magazine publishers that together control half the advertising revenue in the magazine industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 three corporations received half of the $12.6 billion in magazine advertising revenue (Time Warner, Hearst, Advance Publications/Conde Nast changes noted). Track mergers and large acquisitions that rapidly change this count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: radio (ownership and revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess radio consolidation by counting corporations that control a majority of radio revenue and by tracking station-ownership concentrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: by 2009 two companies (Clear Channel Communications and Sirius XM) controlled over half radio revenue; note the role of policy (Telecommunications Act of 1996 removed ownership caps) and station counts (Clear Channel grew from 43 to 850 stations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: network and broadcast television (ad revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure which broadcast networks take in the majority of TV advertising revenue to assess dominance in network television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 CBS, News Corp (Fox) and Walt Disney (ABC) took over half of broadcast TV advertising revenue; the top four with NBC received 70%. Use broadcast ad-revenue shares to identify dominant networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: cable television (ad revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess concentration among cable networks by their share of cable advertising revenue; consider combining broadcast and cable for a larger sector measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 three cable networks (Disney, Time Warner, Viacom) received over half the $49 billion in cable advertising revenue; treating broadcast+cable together shows four companies dominating a $74 billion market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific concentration: book publishing (revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count corporations that together control half the book-sales revenue to evaluate concentration in book publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 five corporations (Bertelsmann/Random House, Pearson, Hachette, News Corp/HarperCollins, CBS/Simon & Schuster) controlled half the $23.9 billion market. Note cross-ownership with other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet/online advertising concentration and algorithmic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure online-ad revenue shares among major internet companies and account for how search algorithms concentrate audience attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in 2009 Google and Yahoo received over half of $20.9 billion online ad revenue; as leading search engines they use commercially driven algorithms that influence how people explore the Web. Include measures of audience share and algorithmic gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience concentration online vs traditional media
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare levels of audience concentration produced by the Internet to those of traditional media to evaluate whether the Internet decentralizes or concentrates attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite research (Matthew Hindman) that finds the Internet produces levels of audience concentration greater than traditional media and disadvantages local content providers. Use audience metrics and distribution of traffic to local vs national outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical integration and cross-ownership as power multipliers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the extent to which corporations hold vertically integrated properties (content + distribution) and cross-ownership across media sectors, increasing their market power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Comcast and AT&T eyeing both infrastructure and content; Comcast purchased NBC and Universal. Vertical integration can position firms above even other powerful media corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory environment and policy changes enabling consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how FCC rules, acts like the 1996 Telecommunications Act, and loosening or repeal of ownership/cross-ownership limits have enabled consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 1996 Act removed most radio ownership caps; FCC changes allowed the Sirius-XM merger. Track policy changes and their timing relative to ownership consolidation trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative scale within the dominant group (not all 'dominant' firms are equally powerful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that within the set of firms that together control half the market, some corporations (e.g., News Corp, Viacom, Bertelsmann, GE, Disney) are substantially more powerful than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example comparison: Hearst's $3B vs Disney's $18B net media revenue in 2009. Use absolute revenue and market position, not only 'count of firms', to characterize dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial model dependence leading to homogenized content
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how an advertising-driven commercial model incentivizes 'lowest common denominator' national fare and undermines diverse, locally relevant, or investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: as companies collect vertically integrated properties, market logic inclines them to produce homogenized national content, neglecting public-interest obligations and investigative journalism. Consider editorial outcomes, program diversity, and investment in local/investigative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localism: number of independent local news outlets and local newspaper availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the health of local news by counting independent local papers per city and assessing concentration at the local level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: major cities like Houston, Seattle, Denver and Cincinnati reduced to one local daily newspaper. Use presence/absence of independent outlets, ownership consolidation at city level, and local newsroom capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of ownership and newsroom representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess ownership demographics (race, gender) and newsroom workforce composition as indicators of viewpoint diversity and representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heads of the 20 corporations were white males; ASNE data: ethnic minorities <13% of newsroom employees, <4% of TV station ownership, <8% of radio station ownership; women 37% of full-time newspaper newsroom staff. Use ownership and staffing metrics to infer limits on 'diverse and antagonistic' voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on democratic values and First Amendment 'freedom to hear'
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how concentration impairs the First Amendment ideal of 'the widest possible dissemination of information from diverse and antagonistic sources' by limiting the freedom to hear diverse voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use normative assessment linked to ownership concentration, lack of newsroom diversity, and diminished localism. Consider legal/regulatory interpretations promoted by large corporations that emphasize their freedom to speak over the public's freedom to hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of new technologies to resist or replicate consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether emergent technologies (cable, satellite radio, Internet) have fulfilled democratic hopes or been subsumed by commercial consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical pattern: new media were idealized but became commercialized and consolidated (radio, TV, cable). For the Internet, evaluate ISP choice concentration (one or two ISPs in many areas), consolidation of online ad revenue, and platform control over content distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical, time-series tracking of consolidation trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Track changes in the number and identity of dominant firms over time to document consolidation dynamics (e.g., 1983 → 1987 → 1993 → 2009 comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article: the number controlling half the media went from 50 people (1983) to 26 (1987) to 20 (1993) and—using updated methods—15 (for legacy sectors) or 20 (including emergent technologies) in 2009. Use consistent methodology to compare over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and data source transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Base concentration claims on transparent, citable data sources (e.g., Advertising Age, Box Office Mojo, Pew Research Center, FCC rulings, ASNE statistics, academic studies) and state the metrics used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article relies on named sources and specific figures (e.g., Advertising Age ad-revenue data, Box Office Mojo box-office figures, Pew for TV news source stats). Ensure sources and measurement choices (revenue vs circulation, ad revenue) are explicit.
